rationale.SE-5: Relaxing a standard without a record hides risk from later reviewers.
rationale.SE-1: Sets the plan every discipline works to; needed before SRR so requirements are written once.
rationale.SE-2: Records why this tiltrotor layout was picked over alternatives.
rationale.SE-3: Every requirement needs a closing method and a baseline to close it against.
rationale.SE-9: New technology is where schedule and performance surprises come from.
rationale.SE-10: TRL 6 at PDR is the common gate before committing to detailed design.
rationale.SE-11: A prediction written after the test cannot show the model was wrong.
rationale.SE-12: A requirement without one shall, a number and a rationale cannot be verified.
rationale.SE-13: Errors found at baselining cost far less than errors found at test.
rationale.SE-14: Driving requirements need early management attention.
rationale.SE-15: Goals and contexts written first keep later requirements tied to why the aircraft exists.
rationale.SE-16: A fixed boundary says what the requirements may and may not talk about.
rationale.SE-17: Use cases expose missing functions before design hardens.
rationale.SE-18: An unstated assumption is a hidden requirement on the environment.
rationale.SE-19: The tilt conversion changes behavior sharply and needs explicit modes.
rationale.SE-20: Specifying outputs with conditions makes gaps and overlaps findable.
rationale.SE-21: Derived requirements must be visible to the owners of the level above.
rationale.SE-22: Allocation without a boundary at each level loses accuracy and timing budget.
rationale.SE-23: Work outside the structure goes unplanned, and a second structure splits cost and technical tracking.
rationale.SE-24: A dictionary entry is what keeps two disciplines from each assuming the other does a task.
rationale.SE-25: Only a statement with a stated way to close it can be verified.
rationale.SE-26: Tracking planned against actual performance shows trouble before the next review.
rationale.SE-27: The checklist catches vague words and open values while they are cheap to fix.
rationale.SE-4: Interfaces between disciplines drift unless a plan is kept current.
rationale.SE-6: The chief engineer owns technical performance and must see it measured.
rationale.SE-7: Review depth scales with risk so effort goes where failure costs most.
rationale.SE-8: Unfiltered escalation stops technical issues being softened on the way up.
rationale.AER-11: Sensor error propagates into every derived coefficient.
rationale.AER-12: Agreement between techniques is the check on each one.
rationale.AER-13: Flight data without metadata cannot be reused.
rationale.AER-14: Two codes agreeing guards against a single-code error; the drag tolerance is a starting value.
rationale.AER-3: Users of the model need uncertainty and axes to apply it correctly.
rationale.AER-4: Sign and axis errors are a common cause of wrong results.
rationale.AER-5: CFD on wrong geometry gives precise but wrong answers.
rationale.AER-6: Results cannot be reproduced without the inputs and code versions.
rationale.AER-7: Instrumentation added late rarely covers the flight objectives.
rationale.AER-8: Air data accuracy limits every derived aerodynamic quantity.
rationale.AER-9: Swapped or mislabeled sensors have lost flight data before.
rationale.AER-10: Flight data is the check on the pre-flight model.
rationale.AER-1: Hover, conversion and cruise are different aerodynamic regimes.
rationale.AER-2: The database must follow the latest CFD and test data to stay usable by loads and flutter.
rationale.LDS-1: Structures needs preliminary loads to size primary structure.
rationale.LDS-7: Mixed units in structural models have caused major losses.
rationale.LDS-2: Limit and ultimate loads close the design load cases.
rationale.LDS-3: Modeling assumptions that change results must be visible to the next user.
rationale.LDS-4: Datasets passed between teams carry silent unit and format errors.
rationale.LDS-5: Single precision and unnormalized shapes corrupt modal data.
rationale.LDS-6: Regression tests catch toolchain changes that move results; tolerance is a starting value.
rationale.STR-3: The factor of safety sets structural mass; 2.25 is a stand-in until the chief engineer chooses.
rationale.STR-4: A limited envelope can substitute for a test where the structure is untested to ultimate.
rationale.STR-1: Margins of safety are the structural closure record.
rationale.STR-2: Analysis applies only to the structure as built.
rationale.SIN-3: Composite strength is shown by building up from coupons to the article; verify factor.
rationale.SIN-4: A proof load that damages the flight article defeats its purpose.
rationale.SIN-5: Inspection intervals need a crack-growth basis, not a guess.
rationale.SIN-1: Criteria fix the factors and load cases everything else is checked against.
rationale.SIN-2: Ground test finds structural problems before flight.
rationale.ROT-1: Rotor loads drive nacelle, wing and flutter results.
rationale.ROT-2: Flutter needs a rotor and nacelle model with stated assumptions.
rationale.FLU-1: Whirl flutter is the instability specific to tilting rotors.
rationale.FLU-2: No single method clears flutter; analysis, GVT and flight test support each other.
rationale.FLU-3: Flutter analysis needs a model of airframe, rotors and nacelles together.
rationale.FLU-5: Control loops can couple with structure; 8 dB and 60 degrees are starting values.
rationale.FLU-6: Mass properties feed the model; measured values beat estimates.
rationale.FLU-8: An uncorrelated model cannot predict flutter; 5 percent and 0.1 are starting values.
rationale.FLU-9: Flutter results go stale when the model changes.
rationale.FLU-10: A flutter flight test needs a plan with build-up and abort criteria.
rationale.FLU-11: Flight is the last check that no instability exists in the envelope.
rationale.FLU-12: A rotating nacelle changes the modes with tilt angle.
rationale.FLU-13: Uncertain parameters bound the envelope instead of hiding in one run.
rationale.FLU-14: Testing can be skipped only with a large margin; 100 percent is a starting value.
rationale.FLU-4: A margin on flutter speed covers model error; 15 percent is a starting value.
rationale.FLU-7: GVT gives the measured modes the model is correlated to.
rationale.FTP-3: Practice in simulation finds problems cheaply.
rationale.FTP-4: Edge-of-envelope points need a planned way out.
rationale.FTP-5: A briefing closes open items before the next flight.
rationale.FTP-7: Instrumentation designed late rarely meets objectives.
rationale.FTP-6: Debrief captures discrepancies while memory is fresh.
rationale.FTP-1: No test point flies without a released plan and card.
rationale.FTP-2: Flight starts only after the operational readiness review closes.
rationale.SOF-3: Severity and probability scoring gives a common risk language.
rationale.SOF-4: Human-safety risk is not the project team's to accept.
rationale.SOF-5: Review level should match complexity and risk.
rationale.SOF-6: Reviewers outside the team give independent judgement.
rationale.SOF-8: A lost link needs a pre-decided response; DAA and BVLOS are not modelled.
rationale.SOF-9: The cited ASTM F3178-16 came from a draft circular and must be checked.
rationale.SOF-10: The remote pilot must always be able to take control.
rationale.SOF-7: Approval needs a written statement of residual risk.
rationale.SOF-1: Hazards must be known before a review can judge them.
rationale.SOF-2: Open hazard items need a recorded disposition.
rationale.CMG-4: The as-built article must link back to design and analysis.
rationale.CMG-5: Simulation changes alter test planning, so they are configuration items.
rationale.CMG-1: The plan states how baselines and changes are handled.
rationale.CMG-2: An unbaselined requirement cannot be verified against.
rationale.CMG-3: Releases must be recorded to know what flew.
rationale.VEH-1: Fixes the configuration every other requirement refers to.
rationale.VEH-2: Sets the battery and power sizing.
rationale.VEH-3: Operation under Part 107 is the project operating basis.
rationale.VEH-3.1: Part 107 limits takeoff mass; margin is a project decision.
rationale.VEH-3.2: Part 107 sets the altitude and groundspeed limits.
rationale.VEH-3.3: Part 107 requires visual line of sight.
rationale.VEH-4: The corridor sets the aerodynamic and control design space.
rationale.VEH-5: Whirl flutter is the main aeroelastic risk of a tilting rotor.
rationale.VEH-6: Factors of safety are not chosen yet.
rationale.VEH-7: Explicit modes keep the conversion from producing undefined behavior.
rationale.VEH-8: Outputs without latency and tolerance cannot be verified.

program: A systems engineering management plan, or equivalent, shall be signed off before SRR.
Conceptual design and trade studies shall be documented and shall recommend one configuration.
The verification and validation plan shall be baselined.
The integration plan shall be updated.
Design standards shall be chosen for the aircraft, and any relaxation shall be recorded with its rationale, such as real-time monitoring or operating limits.
The project chief engineer shall assess technical performance against design allocations, margins and trades every month, and shall report the assessment to the approving authority.
The program shall apply a risk-based method to set how deeply each discipline program is independently reviewed, and the top technical risks shall be reported with each monthly assessment.
Technical issues shall go up the chief engineer chain without filtering, and late-breaking or potential issues shall be briefed to the approving authority before the next review.

New technologies the aircraft needs, such as the tilt mechanism, conversion control and the nose gimbal, shall be identified as critical technology elements and agreed with the approving authority, and an initial technology readiness assessment shall record the readiness level of each.

Each critical technology element shall reach the readiness level below by PDR, the readiness of any assembly shall not be rated above its least mature element, and the assessment shall be updated at PDR.
Analysis predictions shall be recorded before each development test, and a test result outside the predicted uncertainty shall have its variance explained and its root cause reviewed.

Each requirement shall be a complete statement with one shall, a quantitative measure where it states performance, and a recorded rationale that gives the reason, assumptions and link to the concept of operations.

Requirements shall be validated before baselining: written to the form in SE-12, technically correct with bidirectional traceability, accepted by stakeholders, feasible, verifiable, and neither redundant nor over-specified.

Key driving requirements, those that would move cost or schedule by more than the amount the chief engineer sets, shall be identified, and technical performance measures shall be tracked against planned values at each review.
The system overview shall be written before requirements: a synopsis, the operating contexts, a context diagram, the external entities and the preliminary system goals, and it shall be kept current.

The system boundary shall be defined early as the monitored variables the aircraft senses, the controlled variables it commands and the environmental variables it must tolerate, each with type, range, precision and units, and every physical interface shall be defined.

Operational concepts shall be written as use cases titled by their goal and traced to system goals, each with a primary actor, preconditions and postconditions, normal flow first, then exception cases and alternate courses, and without operator interface details.
Each environmental assumption shall state type, range, precision and units, shall carry its rationale, and shall be grouped by the entity it constrains.
Major flight modes and the transitions between them shall be identified, including any mode added for a discontinuity the pilot can see.

Each controlled variable shall be specified as a condition and an assigned value, with its latency and tolerance, and the set shall be complete, consistent and free of duplication; latency and tolerance shall not be set on internal variables.
Each design decision that constrains the design further shall be flagged as a derived requirement, and its latency and accuracy shall be confirmed against the top-level values.

When requirements are allocated to a subsystem, the subsystem shall have its own overview, monitored and controlled variables and operational concept, shared assumptions shall be identified, and latencies and tolerances shall be consistent with the system level.

One product-oriented work breakdown structure shall cover the whole scope of work, including enabling work such as project management and safety, shall be drafted as early as project definition allows, and shall be changed only by formal approval after it is baselined.

A work breakdown structure dictionary shall define each element with its title, code, content, interfaces, associated specification and revision history, shall be clear enough to remove overlap between elements, and shall be a baselined controlled document.

A verification matrix shall list every shall statement by unique identifier, source document and paragraph, with its success criteria, method, facility or laboratory, phase, and whether it is also checked at acceptance and before each flight.

Measures of effectiveness shall be derived from the goals, measures of performance from those, and the technical performance measures that matter to flight success shall be tracked against their planned values at each review.

Each requirement shall be checked before baselining for: active form, a stated tolerance, no implementation, positive wording, no unverifiable terms, and traceability up to a parent and down to a verification; TBD values shall be kept few, each with a best estimate, an owner and a closing review.
An aerodynamic database covering hover, conversion and cruise shall be released.
The database shall be updated with the latest CFD and test data and re-released.
The aerodynamic model shall carry uncertainties, state its axis system, document its limits of use and data sources, and be kept under version control.
CFD shall use one defined coordinate system and sign convention, validated codes, and grid independence studies on the most complex geometry and flow.
The CAD model used for CFD shall be checked against measurements or photographs of the as-built aircraft.
The CAD models, grids, solver settings, scripts, solutions and code versions used in airworthiness reviews shall be archived.
Aerodynamic instrumentation shall be defined early from the project objectives, with sensors sized and calibrated for the full envelope and the worst local environment, and with spare capacity.
Air data accuracy requirements shall be stated before the air data system is designed, and an in-flight calibration shall be planned.
Sensor locations, labels and calibrations shall be checked twice before the flight campaign, and the instrumentation kept under configuration control.
The pre-flight aerodynamic model and its uncertainties shall be validated against flight data during envelope expansion, using more than one parameter estimation method, and updated as needed.
The effect of sensor errors on the derived quantity, such as pressure error on angle of attack, shall be analyzed, and temperature and tubing lag effects shall be accounted for.
Aerodynamic parameters shall be estimated with more than one technique, the differences shall be reviewed for data errors, and reported uncertainties shall be treated as lower bounds.
Flight data shall be archived with metadata, and the steps that convert raw data to engineering data shall be documented.
Two independent CFD codes shall be compared before the production database runs, and each run shall be converged to the drag tolerance below.
Aerodynamic and inertial loads shall be released as a preliminary loads set.
Limit and ultimate loads shall be released for flight and ground conditions under revision control.

Modeling assumptions that change results, such as whether the rotor and nacelle motion is inside or outside the structural modes, shall be documented and shared by the loads, structures and flutter programs.
Sanity checks shall be run on each structural dataset before it is delivered to a downstream user.

Modal data shall keep double precision, and mode shapes shall be mass-normalized so that the transpose of the mode shape matrix times the mass matrix times the mode shape matrix equals the identity matrix.

Regression tests shall exercise the finite element to dynamics model toolchain, and any modal-integral implementation shall be checked against an independent model, with accelerations agreeing within the tolerance below.
Finite element and dynamic models shall use one consistent unit system and a right-handed coordinate system, and the model mass and center of gravity shall be checked against the actual article.
Stress notes shall show margins of safety for all primary structure.
The as-built structure shall be shown to conform to the released drawings.

One static-strength approach shall be selected and documented: no test and no data, test and data, test and no data, or a justified alternative, with an ultimate factor of safety that fits the approach. The factor below is a placeholder until the project selects.
The flight envelope shall be limited to the fraction of limit load that the selected approach supports, and where the aircraft is the proof article it shall be fully instrumented and calibrated.
Structural design criteria shall be defined: factors of safety, load cases and fatigue approach.
A structural ground test shall verify the design before flight.

Composite structure shall be substantiated by a building-block approach: coupon tests, then design-feature tests, then proof loading on the aircraft, with a factor of safety of 3.0 on secondary structure of unproven equivalence.
Where the aircraft is the proof-test article, the proof load shall be applied and its results compared with analysis before first flight.

Inspection intervals shall be set from fatigue-crack growth analysis so that the smallest crack the inspection method can detect cannot grow to failure within the interval, and the interval shall reflect each aircraft's actual usage.
Rotor loads and rotor-induced aerodynamic effects shall be characterised for the loads and aerodynamics programs.
A rotor and nacelle dynamics model shall be released to the flutter program.
The aeroelastic instabilities likely in the flight envelope, including whirl flutter, shall be identified, and any excluded shall be recorded with the reason.
Flutter clearance shall use flutter analysis, ground vibration test and flight flutter test, because the aircraft is new.
A finite element model of the airframe, rotors and nacelles shall be built and its modes calculated; an equivalent-beam model is the minimum.
A preliminary flutter analysis at the key flight points, including whirl flutter across the conversion corridor, shall show at least the margin below on equivalent airspeed and Mach number.
Every feedback loop of the flight control system shall have at least the gain and phase margins below.
Weight, centre of gravity and moments of inertia shall be measured to correlate the model.
A ground vibration test shall measure mode shapes, frequencies and damping in every relevant configuration.
The model shall be correlated to the ground vibration test: frequency error on significant modes at most the first limit below, and off-diagonal orthogonality terms at most the second.
If the structural or aerodynamic model was updated, the flutter analysis shall be repeated at the key flight points.
A flight flutter test plan shall define the instrumentation, build-up test points and real-time monitoring with test point clearance.
Flight flutter testing shall show no instability within the flight envelope, and the models shall be correlated to flight data.
Where body inertia changes with deformation or the nacelle rotates, modal integrals shall be included, and results with and without them shall be compared side by side.

Uncertain model parameters shall be varied to bound the flutter envelope, a margin of at least the largeMarginPercent value shall be confirmed under all variations, and critical parameter combinations shall be identified.
Flight flutter testing shall be omitted only where the margin on a high-confidence model exceeds the value below, and the omission shall be recorded as a deviation.
A flight test plan and test cards shall be released.
No flight shall start until the operational readiness review is closed.
Flight maneuvers and test conditions shall be designed and practised in flight simulation before flight.
The envelope expansion plan shall include a bail-out plan for the edges and corners of the envelope, and shall watch in flight for any cliffs found in CFD or wind tunnel data.
A technical briefing shall close out all open items, peer review the plan and the current risks, and end with signed approval to fly.
Each flight shall be followed by a debrief, and discrepancies and results shall be documented and compared with predictions.
Instrumentation shall be designed early, to show safety, experiment success and experiment failure, and its reliability and maintainability shall be planned for the full program.
A preliminary hazard analysis shall be completed.
A safety of flight review shall be completed with open items dispositioned.

Hazards shall be identified, evaluated for cause and effect, and scored for severity and probability on the hazard scales, with mitigations recorded, and the analysis kept current through the life cycle.
No human-safety risk shall be accepted by the project team; any exception needs a recorded decision by the approving authority named in the configuration management plan.
The level of independent review shall be chosen to match the complexity, criticality and risk of the flights, and the choice recorded.
A flight readiness review by reviewers outside the project team shall examine the analyses, procedures, hazard analyses and qualification results, and the project shall respond to each finding.
A written recommendation quantifying residual risk, with accepted risks named, shall be signed by the approving authority before the first flight.
A lost-link procedure shall be defined with a predesignated contingency landing site and verified in ground and flight test.
The hazard analysis shall follow ASTM F3178-16, which the NASA memo cites for small unmanned aircraft under 55 pounds.
The remote pilot shall be able to command or override the vehicle at all times.
A configuration management plan shall be approved.
The requirements shall be baselined and changed only through change control.
Document, load and data releases shall be recorded, and the design baselined.
Design, analysis and manufacturing shall stay linked so that the as-built performance is confirmed against the analysis.
Flight simulations shall be under version control as part of configuration control.
vehicle: The vehicle shall be a twin-rotor tiltrotor with a gimbal in the nose that carries a replaceable payload sensor, and a separate FPV camera.
Built aircraft matches the configuration drawing: two tilting rotors, a nose gimbal with a replaceable sensor, an FPV camera and landing gear.
The vehicle shall have at least 30 minutes of flight time. Reserve policy to be set.
Hover-and-cruise profile flown to battery cutoff reserve; elapsed flight time at least 30 minutes.
The vehicle shall be operable under 14 CFR Part 107.
Takeoff mass including payload shall be less than the limit, with a sizing margin to be set.
Weighed takeoff mass with payload below 55 lb by the sizing margin.
Operation shall stay below the altitude limit and at or below the groundspeed limit.
Flight data shows altitude never above 400 ft AGL and groundspeed never above 87 kt across the demonstrated envelope.
Operation shall stay within visual line of sight of the remote pilot.
Pilot holds visual contact over all test legs.
The vehicle shall convert between hover and cruise inside a conversion corridor to be defined.
Analysis shows controllable, stable conversion across the corridor with margins in the flight control requirements.
The vehicle shall be free of whirl flutter inside the flight envelope, with at least the margin required in the flutter program requirements.
No unstable mode inside the flight envelope with the margin in the flutter requirements.
The structure shall carry limit loads without detrimental deformation and ultimate loads without failure, with factors to be set.
Positive margin of safety at limit and ultimate load for every load case.
The vehicle shall move between flight modes only along the transitions defined in the FlightModes state definition.
Analysis of the mode logic shows no transition outside the four defined.
Every monitored and controlled variable of the vehicle shall have a unit and range, and every controlled variable shall also have a latency and a tolerance.
Each boundary variable carries a unit and range, and each controlled variable a latency and tolerance.
